name: Snow-block domed shelter
summary: Inuit built domed winter shelters from cut, fitted blocks of packed snow, sometimes laid in a rising spiral, as described by Parry in 1822 and Boas in 1888.
description: Cut, fitted blocks of compacted snow form an inward-rising domed shelter. Courses can be laid in tiers or as a continuous spiral; suitable snow is worked at the winter site, and snow quality and seasonal melting limit use.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.
why: In the Arctic winter, suitable snow was the building material available on the spot, for both settled housing and travel shelters.

places.note: And adjoining Arctic regions; And neighboring central Arctic regions

date.basis: Parry’s account dates the encounter and description of the occupied snow houses to 1 February 1822.

events.statement: On 1 February 1822, Parry described occupied Inuit dwellings at Winter Island whose domed rooms were formed from fitted snow blocks.
events.scope: Fitted snow blocks form domed rooms in an occupied winter village.
events.population: Inuit occupants encountered by Parry on 1 February 1822
events.caveats: The February 1822 account does not explicitly describe a spiral. The 1888 Boas account describes a separate spiral example without establishing when that technique began or a link between individual structures. Stone and earthen domes are distinct comparators; no claim to first vaulting or first shelter is made.

evidence.supports: Describes occupied dwellings with domed rooms made of individual snow blocks.

evidence.locator: Account of the Esquimaux, winter habitations
evidence.supports: Separately describes blocks cut from a drift and fitted in successive inward-inclining tiers to build winter habitations.

date.label: By 1888
date.basis: Boas’s published 1888 ethnography describes construction and use; not every observation is individually dated.

events.statement: Boas describes Central Arctic Inuit construction and use of snow-block domes with a rising spiral course, including winter travel shelters.
events.scope: A dome of cut, fitted blocks of compacted snow placed as an inward-rising spiral course.
applications: Winter travel shelters and seasonal housing
events.population: Central Arctic Inuit builders and users described by Boas
events.caveats: Boas’s book combines his own field observations with other travelers’ reports; the exact date and identity of every construction described are not isolated. Earlier snow houses are not automatically evidence of the spiral technique. Syrian earth domes use a similar spiral course; dates and any relation between the two construction traditions remain unresolved. Snow quality, seasonal melt and local skill limit use; no durable or universal shelter claim is made.

evidence.locator: Printed pp. 539–541, Habitations and dress, The house
evidence.supports: Describes winter snow-block shelters built by a rising spiral course, without scaffold, and used for travel camps.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest defensible dated record of this scoped referent in the retained evidence; later community entry is recorded separately. This is the earliest supported record currently established here, not certification of absolute priority.
